lines: CASTLE HALT. LOST PROPERTY. The office is not staffed. It is still open.
Reported lost and not yet found, all on the station road: one child's glove, red, at the well. One man's felt hat, at the signpost on the same road.
Further along the same road: one carter's dinner tin, by a cart that did not arrive.
All three are beside the road. Finders please enter items below. A pencil is provided.
Glove: the well on the station road. Hat: the signpost on the same road. Tin: the cart further along the station road. The pencil is on its string.
Three lines to fill in. The column headed CLAIMED BY is wider than the others.
Printed at the foot of the page: Finders may take one article from the unclaimed shelf. One.
LEFT LUGGAGE. One trunk, tin-lined, heavy. Consignor: Goldskin Mining Co. To go by the Sunday train.
Held for want of the key, which the carter has. The carter was last seen on the mine road with a full cart, walking beside it, near enough the mine to see it.
The cart is on the mine road, the last stretch before the mine. The trunk has not moved. There is a ring of clean platform round it where nobody has stood.
The trunk is open. Somebody ought to write that down.
In pencil, a different hand: Parcel, brown paper, string. Left by the platform crate each evening after the bell. NOT lost property. Do not hand in. It is collected.
Underneath: would somebody check that it still is.
After the bell, the entry says. Be on the platform when it goes; the parcel is left on the crate there.
There is a column for the checker's initials. Yours would be the first in it.
There is a line for it already: one haversack, canvas, walker's. Reported lost by the owner, in person, on a date that has not happened yet.
Parcel: collected. Parcel: collected. Parcel: collected. The entries go back further than the book does.
Parcel: NOT collected. Enquiries are being made.
CASTLE PARISH COUNCIL. PUBLIC FOOTPATH No. 3, Castle to Lowfield Farm by the Long Hedge. A right of way lapses if nobody walks it within the year. Nobody has been free.
12 minutes. Longer in the evening.
Footpath No. 3. The stile is past the last house on the farm side.
CASTLE ALLOTMENT SOCIETY. Rats in the sheds again. Members are asked to deal with any they see. Six would be a start.
The Society's ground is out past the last house: fenced plots either side of a cinder path.
The Society notes that they did not use to be this size.

Six would be a start, it says. The allotments are out past the last house: a fingerpost says ALLOTMENTS where the path leaves Castle. Plots either side of a cinder path, and the shed at the end of it.
A second sheet behind the first, and a key pinned under it for the shed. Members only. Anyone who has dealt with six is a member.
CASTLE ALLOTMENT SOCIETY. Plot 9 is not let. Members are reminded not to dig it.
Would whoever digs it each night please stop, or else apply for it in the usual way.
Plot 9 is the one with no name on the stake. By day there is nobody there. The earth is soft.
Someone has written under the notice, small: thank you. he was secretary for eleven years.
CASTLE PARISH COUNCIL. No further notices. The drawing pins have been left in rows.
One notice has been taken down in a hurry. The corner still pinned to the board says SCHOOL.
PLOT 9. Somebody is working it.
PLOT 9. No name on the stake. The soil has been turned today, a spade's depth, in rows.
Who is that. No, I can hear you are not from here. You will be Julie's girl.
I would come out, only I am in the middle of something.
There are three scarecrows on this farm. Gate, Long Hedge, top field. Walk round and count them for me while it is light. I know it is three. I would like to hear it from someone else.
Gate, hedge, top field. The gate one is on the road. The hedge one is in the Long Hedge, off the footpath.
The top field is up the farm track, off the road. There is a post at the bottom of it that says TOP FIELD. You will see the rows before you see the scarecrow. Stay on the rim, mind.
Three. Good. That is the right number for the daytime.
Now I need them counted after the bell. Same three.
Touch the rim of the top field and come straight back. Do not go in among the rows. What is growing in there is not what I planted, and it is worse at night.
If you would rather not, I understand. I would rather not.
After the bell. I will be up. I am always up.
I sit in the back kitchen, the side away from the School. You can see it from the front. I do not need to see it.
Three after dark as well. Thank you.
You would tell me if it were four.
Those things in the top field. I count six from the upstairs window, and they are nearer the yard than they were on Sunday.
It is past anything I would ask of a stranger. I am asking because there is nobody else, and I will not pretend that is the same as it being safe.
By day. Not after the bell. If it goes badly, the fire in my yard is yours.
I can still see them from the window. They do not move while I watch. I cannot watch all the time.
I counted none this morning. First time since the spring.
There is a jar on the step. The last of what my wife put up, the year Julie showed her how. Eat it all. It does not keep once it is open.
Still in the middle of something. You know where the fire is.
One. Somebody has done up the top button of its coat.
A scarecrow. One. Straw, a sack, a coat somebody wore for years.
Two.
Two. The same straw, the same sack, the same coat.
Three. Straw, an old coat, a sack for a head. The rows behind it are not still.
Three. It stands where the field ends. Behind it the rows are full of something round and orange, and the farmer said turnips.
A road atlas of somewhere else. A district nurse's visiting list on a clipboard. The car keys are not here.
Tues. Mrs Allen, Sallow Bottom: dressing. Mr Pike, by the Long Hedge: chest. The Misses Crane, under Quarry Steps: leave it on the step, do not go in.
None of the three is ticked.
Allen, Pike, Crane. Her pencil is still clipped to the board.
Three ticks. Under the clipboard there was a second sheet all along, folded small.
In her hand: If I am not back by dark, do not come and look. I mean it kindly. The wood behind the car is not the wood in front of it.
Her case is on the ground by the car, locked. Her coat is gone. There are prints behind the car, a woman's shoe, going in. They are not hurried. None come back.
Behind the car, she wrote. Not in front. The prints go in among the trees and do not come back. Follow them: the coat is at a hollow tree at the end of them, a hundred paces and more from here.
The case is open on the seat.
A road atlas of somewhere else. The clipboard has gone back under the seat where you found it, though you do not remember putting it there.
Nurse: gone to my sister's in Castle till it passes. Hers is the door facing the fire in the square. Thank you for coming out all this way. E. Allen.
NURSE. Knock twice and wait. If it is after nine do not knock. I will not know it is you. PIKE.
Eleven parcels round the step in the nurse's wrapping, none opened. The oldest has moss on it. A card has been pushed out under the door: NEXT TIME PLEASE BRING YOUR BAG. M. AND E. CRANE.
Is that the nurse? No. You do not walk like the nurse.
Put it through the flap, would you. I am not opening this door until it passes, and my sister agrees with me. Or she did.
Here. Julie brought me these the last winter she was about. I have not the stomach for it now. You look as if you have been walking.
We are not seeing anyone, thank you. Lovely evening. You will want to be in before the lamps.
The dressing is a great comfort. Nurse will be along on Tuesday, I expect. She always is.
Is there a light on up at the School tonight? No, do not tell me. My sister says I am not to ask.
A. PELL. LAMPMAN TO THIS PARISH 31 YEARS. WENT OUT FROM THIS LAMP TO SEE TO No. 14.
Underneath, scratched later: they are numbered from the square. count them if you like.
WENT OUT FROM THIS LAMP TO SEE TO No. 14. The road beyond it has posts and no light.
Twelve, thirteen, fifteen. The stone says he went to see to No. 14.

A parish notice under the stone, newer: THE LAMPMAN'S BRAZIER stands on this road past No. 15, and is to be kept laid. Two planks and a fire stone. Any passer-by may light it, and the parish will be obliged.
Lit, it would be the first light past No. 15, and the nearest fire to the east Lowfields.
A. PELL. LAMPMAN TO THIS PARISH 31 YEARS. Somebody has put a fire stone chip on top of the stone, the way you would a pebble.
No. 12. Dark. The glass is whole and the mantle is new.
A lamp post. No. 12 on the plate. By day there is no telling whether it works.
No. 13. Dark. There are fresh ladder marks on the post.
A lamp post. No. 13 on the plate. By day there is no telling whether it works.
No. 15. Dark. It stands one lamp's distance from No. 13. There is no gap where a lamp could have been. The only light you can see from here is one window of the School, a long way north on its hill.
A lamp post. No. 15 on the plate. By day there is no telling whether it works.
Two planks, one fire stone.
A ring of stones, swept out, with a dry place beside it for planks. It has been kept ready by someone with nothing to put in it.
{name}: the cellar bed is for winter. In summer the white water roses are better wild. Sallow Bottom, on the water, below the jetty, where the bank is soft.
Mrs Allen's cottage is the nearest door to it, if you come by the road. Three is plenty. Pick them before the bell. I never learned what happens after, and I never needed to. J.
Sallow Bottom, on the water, below the jetty. Mrs Allen's is the nearest door. Three. Before the bell. J.
The next page has been turned down for you. There are two rocks and two vials of water on the ground by the book that you would swear were not there this morning.
Rock breaks to stone at the bench. Stone, water, white rose: Stone Skin. For when running is no longer an option.
Keep one by the door. Show the dog. The dog will want to see it. J.
Stone, water, white rose. Show the dog. J.
Show the dog, it says. The step is empty until six.
The rest of the book is planting dates. The last entry is for a Sunday and says only: bulbs in. she will be here before they are up.
GOLDSKIN MINING Co. QUARRY GANG (5 MEN) STOOD DOWN UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE. Any man found working Quarry Steps will be paid off at this hatch.
QUARRY STEPS: THE CUT FACE IN THE FOOTHILLS. THE QUARRY TRACK RUNS FROM THIS YARD TO THE GANG'S CAMP AT THE FOOT OF IT.
The gang has been told. The gang is still working.
5 MEN. Quarry Steps is the cut face up in the foothills. The quarry track goes from this yard to their camp at the foot of it.
You can hear picks when the wind is right. They keep very good time.
The hatch is open. Five pigeonholes, five packets, five names. Nobody is behind the counter to stop you.
GOLDSKIN MINING Co. QUARRY GANG (5 MEN) STOOD DOWN. Someone has added in pencil: and stayed down. thank you.
QUARRY STEPS. GANG OF 5. Dinners: 5. Up at seven: 5. Down at five: 4.
Foreman to see about it.
Five tins are laid out by the cold fire. Four have been eaten from.
Up at seven: 5. Down at five: 4. The steps start behind the camp.
There is room on the slate under the last line, and a stub of chalk.
Down at five: 4. Under it, in your writing: found. Under that, not in your writing, a tick.
QUARRY STEPS. GANG OF 5. Dinners: 5. Up at seven: 5. Down at five: 4. You can hear them working above.
A rock across the adit mouth. Too big to shift and too neat to have fallen. It would take something sudden.
A card in a tin frame, and a pencil on a string.
PUBLIC FOOTPATH No. 3. A card in a tin frame for walkers to date. It has been a long time between walkers.
Horse would not go past the quarry turning. Gone up on foot to see what it is looking at. Back directly.
CASTLE PARISH. THE WELL ON THE STATION ROAD. Drawn at your own risk since the mains came.
A child's red glove lies by the well wall, laid out flat to dry. It has been dry for a long time.
Away north over the fields there is a big building on a hill, with one window lit. It is the only light in that direction.
CASTLE PARISH. THE WELL ON THE STATION ROAD. Drawn at your own risk since the mains came. The bucket is down the shaft and the rope is coiled on the wall.
CASTLE HALT one way. CASTLE the other. The post was painted this year.
A man's felt hat lies at the foot of the post, brim up. The inside of it is dry.
CASTLE HALT one way. CASTLE the other. There is a clean ring on the arm for Castle, where something has been sitting out of the rain.
A carter's cart left on the station road with nothing in the shafts. The sacks are still roped down, and grass has come up through the spokes.
A dinner tin lies in the road beside it.
A carter's cart left on the station road with nothing in the shafts. The sacks are still roped down, and grass has come up through the spokes.
A full cart standing in the ruts on the mine road. Nothing is in the shafts and the load is still roped down.
The carter's key is on the ground by the tailboard.
A full cart standing in the ruts on the mine road, still roped down. The ruts under the wheels have filled in and dried.
CASTLE one way. LOWFIELD FARM the other. A third arm has been taken off and the bolt left in.
There are tyre ruts turning off the road here, into the wood, and they do not come out again. A district nurse parked here and walked in.
SALLOW BOTTOM. PARISH JETTY. Boats to be drawn up by dark. Please do not pick the white roses after dark.
LOWFIELD FARM. TOP FIELD. Turnips. Walkers keep to the headland.
TOP FIELD, by the farm track. Private. Please keep to the track.
PUBLIC FOOTPATH No. 3. THE LONG HEDGE. Castle one way, Lowfield Farm the other. Walkers are asked to keep to the path after dark.
CASTLE ALLOTMENT SOCIETY. MEMBERS ONLY. Plots 1 to 12. Plot 9 is not let.
ALLOTMENTS. Castle Allotment Society. Members and their guests. Gates shut at dusk.
CASTLE PARISH GRAVEYARD. Closed for burials. The footpath behind the graveyard is not a right of way and is not maintained, and it is used.
GOLDSKIN MINING Co. QUARRY STEPS, by the quarry track. Quarry gang only. Gang stood down.
UNCLAIMED. A lamp stone, two bottles of water tied at the necks, and a paper bag of grapes that have not gone off.
A card: FINDERS ONLY. ONE ARTICLE EACH. SEE THE BOOK.
UNCLAIMED. A lamp stone, two bottles of water tied at the necks, and a paper bag of grapes that have not gone off.
A card: FINDERS ONLY. ONE ARTICLE EACH. Your three lines are in the book.
One article. The water, then?
One article. The grapes?
You take one article. Nobody is there to see which.
The shelf, less one article. The gap where it stood has already been dusted round.
